---
title: "Week 10 — Writing, influence and relationships"
description: "How LLM assistance enters interpersonal communication"
---

## This week’s sociological question

<div class="chapter-question">What happens to social relationships when people use LLMs to help them communicate, interpret others and manage interpersonal interactions?</div>

## Connection to the preceding material

Week 9 examined LLM assistance inside a labour process. It separated performance while the system is available from knowledge demonstrated without it, and asked how assistance redistributes expertise, discretion and authority. Week 10 follows the model into interpersonal communication. Here the relevant social organization is the relationship between sender and recipient. A linguistically effective message can still be relationally inappropriate; a persuasive message can still fail to repair an obligation.

The class does not concern AI companionship or the replacement of human confidants. Its object is communication between people when an LLM helps one of them formulate, interpret or manage the exchange.

## Learning outcomes

By the end of the class, you should be able to:

- explain Zelizer’s argument against separate-spheres and hostile-worlds accounts;
- use Goffman and Garfinkel to identify the expectations that organize an interpersonal message;
- distinguish surface acting, deep acting, outward expression and recipient interpretation;
- distinguish generated writing, influence on a writer and interpersonal consequences;
- explain the difference between actual and suspected smart-reply use in Hohenstein et al.;
- explain a default Boolean parameter, keyword arguments and the first `enumerate()` iteration without treating model output as evidence of human sincerity or relationship quality.

## Essential readings and what each contributes

::: {.reading-list}
- **Relational sociology:** Zelizer (2012), “How I Became a Relational Economic Sociologist and What Does That Mean?”, *Politics & Society* 40(2): 145–174. Read the complete article. Zelizer asks how people differentiate ties and match them with transactions, media and meanings. This is the conceptual basis for asking what it means to delegate or mediate an apology, rather than merely whether the wording changes. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1177/0032329212441591). [@Zelizer2012Relational]
- **AI suggestions inside an interaction:** Hohenstein et al. (2023), “Artificial Intelligence in Communication Impacts Language and Social Relationships,” *Scientific Reports* 13: 5487. Read the complete article. The experiments distinguish smart-reply availability, actual use, suspected use, conversational language and partner judgments. [Open article](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-30938-9). [@HohensteinEtAl2023]
- **Influence on the writer:** Williams-Ceci et al. (2026), “Biased AI Writing Assistants Shift Users’ Attitudes on Societal Issues,” *Science Advances* 12(11): eadw5578. Read the complete article. The outcome is the writer’s own attitude after assisted composition, not recipient persuasion or relationship maintenance. [Open article](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adw5578). [@WilliamsCeciEtAl2026]
:::

## Additional readings grouped by purpose

- **Corrective interaction:** Goffman (1955), “On Face-Work.” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/00332747.1955.11023008). [@Goffman1955FaceWork]
- **Background expectations in ordinary interaction:** Garfinkel (1967), *Studies in Ethnomethodology*, chapter 2. [@Garfinkel1967Studies]
- **Emotion work and feeling rules:** Hochschild (1979), “Emotion Work, Feeling Rules, and Social Structure.” [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1086/227049). [@Hochschild1979EmotionWork]
- **Surface and deep acting:** Hochschild (1983), *The Managed Heart*, chapter 3. [@Hochschild1983ManagedHeart]
- **Relational work in legal and historical evidence:** Zelizer (2005), *The Purchase of Intimacy*. [Publisher](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691139364/the-purchase-of-intimacy). [@Zelizer2005Purchase]
- **Media ideologies:** Gershon (2010), *The Breakup 2.0*. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.7591/9780801458002). [@Gershon2010Breakup]

## Sociological and methodological background

The worked case is a condolence message. A close colleague's mother has died after a short illness. The sender knew that she had been ill but never met her. The sender asks an LLM to draft a private message and to offer practical help with seminar notes. The resulting message could have been written entirely by the sender, substantially revised, copied without revision or sent automatically by a system trained on the sender's writing. The recipient could receive the same words in every case.

Goffman helps identify condolence as an interactional obligation. The message recognizes a loss and displays an appropriate orientation towards the bereaved person. Garfinkel's breaching demonstrations appear as a short methodological sidebar. Acting like a lodger at home, demanding precise definitions of ordinary remarks or bargaining over fixed prices produces confusion because it violates rules that participants normally take for granted. A recent social-media prank offers a lighter contemporary illustration: men call male friends simply to say good night, producing laughter, suspicion or concern because the call violates expectations about ordinary reasons for contacting one another. The lecture then returns to the condolence case without treating it as a breaching experiment.

Hochschild moves the analysis from public expression to the management of feeling. Surface acting changes the display. Deep acting attempts to produce or intensify the feeling that the situation calls for. An LLM may merely supply conventional language, help a sympathetic person find words, prompt reflection on the recipient's loss or allow the sender to avoid the expressive task. The generated message cannot distinguish these processes. Evidence about the sender is required. Evidence from the recipient is required to establish how the message was interpreted.

Zelizer's direct object is economic exchange, not AI-mediated communication. Her contribution is the observation that the meaning of a transfer depends on the relationship, payment medium and shared understanding. The same sum can be reimbursement, a gift or repayment. We extend that question cautiously to a condolence message: what act is being performed, through which medium and within which relationship?

Gershon supplies the more direct bridge to AI. Media ideologies are socially learned beliefs about what a medium communicates in addition to its literal content. AI assistance introduces another part of the production process. Its meaning may depend on whether the sender edited the message, whether assistance was disclosed and what the recipient believes about authorship and effort. A model that perfectly mimics the sender's voice would hide stylistic evidence of assistance without resolving these relational questions.

The coding exercise broadens the comparison beyond the opening message. Students record how they would respond to a bereaved colleague, a dispute over workplace credit and a request to protect private family information. They then audit model advice about the same cases. This keeps the student's judgment separate from model output and from any claim about a correct social response.

## Synthesis of the current LLM literature

Hohenstein and colleagues place smart replies inside a live conversation. In Study 1, 219 pairs discussed a policy issue and each partner was independently assigned access or no access to smart replies. The system recorded actual use. Random availability was used as an instrument when estimating the effects of use. Partners of people who used smart replies reported greater cooperation and affiliation. The paper also measured whether participants suspected that their partner had used smart replies. Greater suspected use was associated with less cooperation and affiliation and greater dominance after accounting for actual use. Because suspicion was measured rather than randomly disclosed, this second comparison is correlational. Study 2 randomized the type of suggestions and showed that the suggestions altered the emotional language used in the conversation.

Williams-Ceci and colleagues identify a different pathway. Across two preregistered experiments, participants wrote about societal issues with or without biased autocomplete suggestions and then reported their own attitudes. The suggestions shifted writers’ reported attitudes. The finding concerns influence during composition. It does not show that another person was persuaded, that a message was sincere or that a relationship changed.

Neither contemporary paper offers a sociology of established relationships. Hohenstein et al. observe language and immediate partner judgments in a bounded interaction. Williams-Ceci et al. observe the writer after assisted composition. The historical sociology identifies what remains unmeasured: relationship-specific obligations, feeling rules, beliefs about the production medium and consequences over time.

## Take-home exercise

Record how you would respond to at least one of three social situations before viewing model advice. Run the model for the condolence, workplace-credit and private-information cases, then complete one audit record for each. In your narrated recording, explain the first `enumerate()` iteration, default Boolean, keyword arguments, raw return and final audit dictionary. Identify where the model's response fits or differs from your own, whether it changed your judgment and why your answer is a situated comparison rather than a gold standard.

Use the [recording and submission instructions](../recording-and-submission.qmd), name the file with your name and `Week10`, and submit by **5:00 p.m. Eastern on the Tuesday before the next class**.

## Summary and preparation for next week

LLM assistance can change the language used to perform an interpersonal obligation and may influence the person composing the message. How the resulting message is understood can depend on the tie, the medium and what participants believe about authorship. Evidence about the generated message is not evidence that the recipient accepted it or that the relationship was repaired. Week 11 turns to language, inequality and institutional power.
